title: South Carolina Moped Laws: License, Registration, Helmets, and What Happens After a Crash
excerpt: South Carolina moped laws require a license at 15 or older and registration with the DMV, but a moped is not required to be titled or insured — S.C. Code §§ 56-1-1720 and 56-2-3010. A helmet is required only under 21. Here is each rule with its section, and how a violation gets used against you after a crash.
content:
South Carolina moped laws require a license, require registration, and require a helmet only for riders under 21. You need a valid driver's license or a moped operator's license, which the state issues at 15 — S.C. Code § 56-1-1720. The moped itself must be registered with the Department of Motor Vehicles, and it is not required to be titled or insured — § 56-2-3010.

What counts as a moped in South Carolina

A moped in South Carolina is a cycle the Code expressly defines as a motor vehicle: three wheels or fewer, with or without pedals, powered either by a motor of fifty cubic centimeters or by an electric system designed for an input over 750 watts and no more than 1,500 watts — S.C. Code § 56-1-10(26).

According to the South Carolina Legislative Services Agency's published Title 56 definitions, the same section places electric-assist bicycles outside that definition: with operable pedals, no more than 750 watts and under 20 mph on motor power, they "are not mopeds" (§ 56-1-10(29), read 2026-09-19).

An electric cycle that exceeds those e-bike thresholds may be reclassified as a moped, which must be registered but is not required to be titled or insured — § 56-2-3010; our e-bike accident lawyers page explains where that line sits. An input above 1,500 watts falls outside the moped definition as well.

South Carolina moped rules at a glance

The statewide rules sit in two places: the license sections at S.C. Code §§ 56-1-1720 and 56-1-1730, and the moped article at §§ 56-2-3000 through 56-2-3080.

RuleWhat the statute saysSection
LicenseA valid driver's license or a moped operator's license, issued at 15 or older§ 56-1-1720
RegistrationRegistered and licensed with the DMV like a passenger vehicle; not titled or insured; exempt from property tax§ 56-2-3010
HelmetOperator or passenger under 21 wears a § 56-5-3660 helmet§ 56-2-3070(C)
Riders under 16Daylight hours only, unless accompanied by a licensed driver 21 or older with at least a year of driving experience§ 56-1-1720(B)
Lane, speed, lightsFarthest right lane on a multilane highway; 35 mph maximum; no highway posted above 55 mph, though you may cross one; lights on at all times§ 56-2-3070(B), (D)–(F)

According to the South Carolina Legislative Services Agency's published text of the moped article, violating that operation section is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not more than two hundred dollars or thirty days (§ 56-2-3070(G), read 2026-09-19).

Who may ride, and at what age

You may ride a moped in South Carolina at 15 or older, holding either a valid driver's license or a moped operator's license — S.C. Code § 56-1-1720(A). The moped license stands on its own: a person is eligible "without regard to" the status of any other license, and the DMV may suspend or revoke it only for moped violations — § 56-1-1730.

According to the South Carolina General Assembly's record for H. 3247, this licensing scheme was signed on May 19, 2017 as 2017 Act No. 89 and took effect on November 19, 2018.

Registration, title, and insurance

A moped operated on a public highway must be registered and licensed with the Department of Motor Vehicles in the same fashion as a passenger vehicle — S.C. Code § 56-2-3010(A). Mopeds are not required to be titled or insured in this State — § 56-2-3010(C).

That matters more than any other rule here, because no liability policy is required on the moped itself. The coverage question usually turns on uninsured and underinsured motorist benefits, and S.C. Code § 38-77-30 says mopeds "are considered to be motor vehicles for the purposes of uninsured motor vehicle insurance coverage and underinsured motor vehicle insurance coverage only."

Helmets on a moped

A moped operator or passenger under 21 must wear a protective helmet — S.C. Code § 56-2-3070(C), which requires one "identical to underage motorcycle helmet requirements provided in Section 56-5-3660": a type approved by the Department of Public Safety. At 21 and older, riding bare-headed breaks no South Carolina law.

Both helmet sections are silent on evidence, fault and damages, so a missing helmet is the insurer's comparative-fault argument to prove — never an automatic bar. Our South Carolina helmet laws page gives the rule for every vehicle type.

If you are hurt in a moped crash

A moped crash is a negligence claim in South Carolina: you prove that someone else's carelessness caused your injuries, and you recover as long as you are less than 51% at fault, under Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co. The filing deadline is three years from the date of injury — S.C. Code § 15-3-530.

Because § 56-1-10(26) defines a moped as a motor vehicle, state traffic laws apply to the rider, including DUI — and an adjuster will comb the moped article for the violation that moves your percentage: an unregistered moped, a road posted above 55 mph, a 17-year-old with no helmet. Each is an argument the insurer has to prove, not a bar.

Graeham C. Gillin, a partner and the Chief Operating Officer at Roden Law who handles the firm's South Carolina injury cases, points out that these claims turn on the physical record — registration paperwork, posted speed limits and the damage pattern — long before anyone argues percentages.

According to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety's state-by-state fatality figures, 1,038 people died in South Carolina motor-vehicle crashes in 2024 (2024 FARS data) — the traffic a 35 mph machine with no cage or airbags shares. Our South Carolina motorcycle accident lawyers page explains how a two-wheel claim is built, as does our page on electric scooter accident claims.

How the rule differs across the state line

Georgia requires every moped operator and passenger to wear a helmet at any age, so a rider who is legally bare-headed in South Carolina is breaking the law the moment the moped crosses the state line. The Georgia rule is covered on our Georgia moped laws page.

You may ride at 15 or older with a driver's license or a moped operator's license — S.C. Code § 56-1-1720. Mopeds must be registered like passenger vehicles but are "not required to be titled or insured" — S.C. Code § 56-2-3010. A helmet is required for any operator or passenger under 21 — S.C. Code § 56-2-3070(C). A moped may not exceed 35 mph, or use a highway posted above 55 mph — S.C. Code § 56-2-3070(D), (E). File a South Carolina injury lawsuit within three years — S.C. _roden_faqs.question: Do you need a license to drive a moped in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. S.C. Code § 56-1-1720(A) requires a valid driver's license or a moped operator's license, which the DMV may issue at 15 or older. Section 56-2-3000 requires you to carry that license and the registration on a public highway.

_roden_faqs.question: Do mopeds have to be registered and insured in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Registered, yes; insured, no. A moped on a public highway must be registered and licensed with the DMV like a passenger vehicle — S.C. Code § 56-2-3010(A) — but mopeds are "not required to be titled or insured in this State" (§ 56-2-3010(C)). They count as motor vehicles for uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage only (§ 38-77-30).

_roden_faqs.question: How fast can a moped legally go in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: No faster than 35 mph. S.C. Code § 56-2-3070(D) caps moped speed at thirty-five miles per hour, and § 56-2-3070(E) keeps mopeds off any highway posted above fifty-five, though a rider may cross one at an intersection. On a multilane highway the moped must stay in the farthest right lane except to turn left or when that lane is unsafe.

_roden_faqs.question: Do you have to wear a helmet on a moped in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Only under 21. S.C. Code § 56-2-3070(C) requires a helmet for any moped operator or passenger under twenty-one, meeting the § 56-5-3660 motorcycle standard. At 21 and older a rider may legally ride without one, and neither section makes helmet use a question of fault.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a moped injury lawsuit in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Three years from the date of injury, under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. Waiting costs evidence too, because mopeds get repaired or sold. Fault is decided under Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.: you recover if you are less than 51% at fault. Our South Carolina personal injury FAQ covers fault and damages.
